To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the proteoglycants of the human cartilaginous intervertebral disc end‐plate (a) change with ageing, and (b) differ from those of healthy disc end‐plates.
the proteoglycanes of the cartilagenous end‐plate of healthy discs differ from those of degenerated discs.
the proteoglycants of the cartilagenous endplate of human intervertebral discs change after maturity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the proteoglycanes of the intervertebral disc, and the cartilagious end plate in particular.
the PGs of cartilage and the cartilage end‐plate.
the biochemical and biomechanical aspects of ageing and degeneration in the human intervertebrals disc, and with the possible involvement of the cartilagenous end‐plate in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CEP PGs of degenerated discs are different in several respects from those of healthy CEPs, but the nature of the difference(s) is not yet known.
the PGs of CEP change with ageing/degeneration, but it is not possible at this time to determine the precise nature of the change.
the PGs of degenerated discs are less hydrated, more keratan sulphate rich, and more heterogeneous.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the human intervertebraldisc, there is a continuous gradient in the PGs from the nucleus to the anulus, and from the young to the degenerated disc.
the PGs of healthy discs were similar to those of the nucleus and the anulus; the PGs of degenerated discs were more like those of the nucleus.
the CEP is a complex tissue which is not a mere continuation of the vertebral bone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PGs of CEP change with age and degeneration, suggesting that CEP participates in degeneration process.
the CEP of a degenerated disc contains PGs that resemble those of the nucleus and the anulus in both number and size.
the proteoglyc can composition of the cartil aginous end‐plate is not constant but changes with ageing/degeneration of the disc.
